title: Senior's toolkit: stepping through branches and loops
summary: Conditional and hit-count breakpoints, Watch and Immediate, logpoints, switch refactorings and running one test.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: stepping through branches and loops
steps.body: Control-flow bugs live in one branch or one pass of a loop. Experienced developers do not step through all of it: they stop exactly where it goes wrong and test the fix in isolation.

toolkit.what: Stop only when an expression is true, such as the one order id from the bug report.
flags: right-click the breakpoint > Conditions > Conditional Expression
right-click the gutter > Add Conditional Breakpoint
stop on the Nth pass instead, e.g. `= 500`
(Visual Studio) stop only on one thread or process
toolkit.when: a loop over thousands of items goes wrong for one of them

toolkit.what: Locals shows every variable in scope; Watch keeps any expression you type, re-evaluated at each step. Hover a variable for a quick look, and pin the tooltip to keep it visible.
flags: Debug > Windows > Watch, or right-click an expression > Add Watch
(Visual Studio) QuickWatch: inspect an expression once
Visual Studio shows changed values in red after each step

toolkit.what: Evaluate expressions or call methods while stopped: test a fix to a condition before you edit the code.
flags: Ctrl+Alt+I; prefix with `?` to print a value
calls really run, so `list.Clear()` really clears the list

toolkit.what: Drag the yellow arrow (or Ctrl+Shift+F10 on a line) to run a line again, or skip one, without restarting the program.
flags: move execution back to the `if` to retry it with a changed variable
(Visual Studio) set next statement to the cursor line
right-click > Jump to Cursor (when the debugger supports it)
toolkit.example: Change `hour` to 18 in Locals, drag the arrow back to the if, F10

toolkit.what: Turn a `switch` statement that assigns or returns into a switch expression. The compiler then warns (CS8509) if a value is not covered.
flags: flip a condition and swap the branches
the warning for a switch expression that misses a case
toolkit.example: Cursor on `switch`, Ctrl+., Convert switch statement to expression

toolkit.what: Run only the tests for the branch you are fixing, not the whole suite. (This is the filter syntax of the default VSTest runner; projects that opt into Microsoft.Testing.Platform get framework-specific filter options, listed by `dotnet test --help`.)
flags: every test whose full name contains `Shipping`

steps.prompt: A bug report: "Order 7341 got free shipping but its total is only 12.50." The nightly job loops over 20,000 orders. How do you get to the bad case fastest?
options: A conditional breakpoint on the shipping rule with `order.Id == 7341`, then read Locals and test the condition in the Immediate window
A plain breakpoint and F5 until order 7341 comes round
Print every order's total to the console and search the output
Run the job in Release mode
steps.explain: The debugger checks the condition on every pass and stops only on the order from the ticket. Then you can try the condition's parts in the Immediate window until you see which one is wrong.

steps.prompt: Match the debugger feature to the situation.
pairs: try a different condition while stopped
rerun the `if` after changing a variable
keep an expression visible at every step

steps.prompt: Switch expressions are checked top to bottom. What does this print?
steps.explain: The first arm that matches wins, so `< 20` only sees values that are not below 0. 30 is not below 30, so it falls to `_`. Put the narrowest arms first.

steps.prompt: Run only the tests in `ShippingTests` and show each test's result.
steps.explain: `~` means "contains" and `=` means "exactly". `verbosity=detailed` lists each test instead of only the summary.

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: When a bug report names one item, put its id in a conditional breakpoint before anything else. Use the Immediate window to try a fix to a condition while you are stopped, then lock it in with a test you can rerun with `--filter`.
